text: I used to work at a very large manufacturing facility that was built in the late 1960s. This place was so big it had it's own power substation. They had incredible milling machines to create large parts for aircraft. At some point they were experiencing a large lagging power factor issue and the utility was going to require them to pay for a major upgrade to the power lines to the facility. One of their electrical engineers said hold on. He designed a system to use synchronous motors to create a leading power factor to correct the problem. He used these motors to power air compressors for the facility since they used a lot of compressed air. In 1980 we installed a 5000v 500 horsepower synchronous motor. It was the 3rd compressor in that building. Since that time a lot of the electrical loads have been changing. The lighting all changed from fluorescent to high pressure sodium in 1982. By 1990 we were replacing those with metal halide. Now those have been replaced with LEDs. The milling machines are all going to variable frequency drives. I retired in 2012 so I don't see what's going on there anymore.

From what I've read the real problem with uncorrected electronic power supplies is the amount of third harmonic current drawn, as in a three phase system the neutral current is supposed to cancel but the 3rd harmonics add.

One possible unfortunate unintended consequence is that with the power supply industry bragging about 0.98+ power factors in single phase equipment and crazy low harmonics it has caused a problem for the designers of multi-kilowatt systems.
It is easy to get a simple three phase rectifier to about 0.85, maybe 0.9 I can't remember the exact figure by just levelling the current drawn and sometimes an inductor is enough, but getting above that to the levels claimed for single phase designs is significantly more complicated. As a result installations that should be three-phase input end up using multiple single phase modules instead. Hopefully they are properly spread across phases.

text:
This issue became a big thing when computers first started hitting desktops in large office environments. There were instances of neutral cables actually getting hot enough to burn off their insulation. This is due to the fact that the narrow current pulses that result from simple rectification and capacitive filtering, as shown in the video, don't cancel in three-phase systems and instead almost 100% of the current would flow in the neutral contuctor - six non-overlapping pulses per cycle.

A lot of this was blamed on the use of switched mode power supplies, but any capcitively filtered rectifier circuit is just about as bad. Iron core transformers do slightly knock down the current peaks due to leakage inductance, but not in a very useful way. It was mostly just the fact that switchers were used in most of the devices installed when use of electronics in offices exploded.

text:
Antenna design is kind of an art.  There's some theories out there.  They kind of work.

There are two things about antennas.  First is that all objects have an inductance and capacitance (which is what an antenna is).  Length of an antenna corresponds to a value of inductance and capacitance.  This also gets into wavelength.  All of these factors become inter-related and everything becomes proportional to 1/4 of the wavelength (rise to peak, drop to zero, drop to trough, rise to zero in a sinusoid).  It... is and isn't complicated.  You're charging an extremely small capacitor that discharges across the inductance of itself, forming a tiny tank circuit.  Because all of this corresponds to distance, you can get weird phenomena like reflections (you can "kink" high frequency electricity like you would a garden hose), standing waves (why putting metal in a microwave leads to arcing), etc.

The second thing is that stripline works by preserving the symmetry of transverse modes... while microstrip makes a great antenna because it does away with said symmetry.

To my knowledge, there is not, as of yet, a "theory of everything" for the electromagnetic spectrum.  When does a tank circuit couple fields versus produce photons... and is it photons mediating between the coils of transformers?

text: A very good explanation of the efficiency of the used electrical energy.  The problem that arises is with dirty input energy.  Where various devices connected to the network leave traces in the form of high-frequency harmonic oscillation.  These phenomena are best observed in high-rise buildings with several apartments, which are connected to a single transformer station!  Another point that you can show is at what DC input voltage the device starts working normally and if the components can withstand the DC stress.  Capacitors are not the best friends with direct current because it fills them up and doesn't let them breathe, causing them to burn out.  And manufacturers use these stress statistics to make products with an approximate lifespan of around 5 years of constant use.  However, coils have an enemy in high-frequency pulses, because their property is inductive in nature, they create counter currents and amplification of the electromagnetic field from the surroundings into the very circuit that we use.  So that in a society with more and more devices that use wireless technology, it is necessary to protect the coils from the signal-filled environment.  It would be nice to have an efficiency coefficient close to 1, but until this is put into law and forces manufacturers to comply, I don't see why they would do it by themselves and guarantee a long working life of the devices.  Just looking at smartphones and computers, even if the device itself is still working after 5 years, we now have to throw it in the trash because there is no software support, and spare parts stop being produced after 3 years of the product release!  And let's not forget that just one such device usually costs at least two salaries of an average working person.  And everything that is cheaper no longer has service or software support!

It is interesting that this video is saying almost exactly the same things that were being said a quarter of a century ago. 
That was back when I first undertook the design of a 1kW switcher for a highly specialized purpose and used the Untrode UC3854 for PFC. The 3854 performed really well but the development was pretty painful. There were no development boards around. Just procuring things like inductor cores (I used "Kool Mu", which was pretty new at the time) and high-performance capacitors was a whole lot more complicated and time consuming than it is now. (If I were doing the design now I'd probably go with a PFC stage that used two interleaved converters. They have some significant advantages in situations were high performance and very long service life are necessary.)

One "trick" of active PFC is that the instantaneous input current must be made to be directly proportional to the instantaneous input voltage while the average input current must be made inversely proportional to the input voltage.

text:
It's an inefficiency in the utility's business model to only bill you for active power.  Poor power factor contributes to increased operating expenses of the grid, that are not reflected in the real power your utility measures.  Displacement power is easy to correct for, since you can simply add the opposite circuit element from the problem type of power factor.  Distortion power is much more difficult to correct for, at the utility scale.

It's common that larger customers are billed for power factor and/or reactive power, while for residential customers, it is difficult to justify the expense of upgrading the meter.  That said, it's only a matter of time until there is enough saturation of non-linear loads for it to become a problem that they eventually have to start reflecting in billing, as a motive to the consumer solve the problem.

text:
Power factor is something most people don't worry about because power companies don't bother residential customers about it.  Business customers are scrutinized, and they are penalized if they can't keep the PF above 0.75, or in some places, 0.90, but that's usually only a concern for the building manager.  Historically, business customers had equipment with electric motors (basically inductors) that lowered the PF, while residential customers had mostly resistive lighting and heating with a few motors that turned on periodically (refrigerator, AC, washing machines, etc.).  However, resistive lighting and heating has almost disappeared, replaced by LEDs and heat pumps, and now almost everything we use has an electronic power supply, full of capacitors and inductors.  I don't know what my home's PF is, and the electronic electricity meter that replaced the old analog one doesn't say, but I wouldn't be surprised if that changed.  After all, if power companies switch to time-of-use pricing to reduce maximum demand, they're going to be interested in raising a customers PF for the same reason.
   What really bugs me are LED light bulbs.  The whole point of LED light bulbs is to reduce electricity usage, but manufacturers aren't letting that happen.  Only one watt is needed to produce 200 lumens, but most of the light bulbs I've tested (in the US) get 100 lumens/watt at best.  The excess is turned into heat.  I've measured surface temperatures of over 200 deg F/90 deg C on many bulbs, and the only reason for making them get that hot is to keep the bulb from lasting for a long time.  Heat is the enemy of electronics, but LEDs are cold devices, and especially sensitive to too much heat.  On top of that, most LED light bulbs have a PF of around 0.5, which means the power company has to generate 2 watts for every watt used by the bulb; the extra watt is turned into heat in the power lines.  In extreme cases, this extra heat causes power lines to sag an unsafe amount.  To sum it up, most LED light bulbs, which we use to minimize power usage and reduce global warming, USE 4 TIMES THE ELECTRICITY THAT THEY NEED.  And while most bulbs are less than 20 watts, and used for only a few hours a day in homes, there are millions of them on at any given time.  It adds up.   (I understand the EU has implemented or is implementing requirements that LED light bulbs get 200 lumens/watt.)

text:
Active PFC circuits can be very difficult in terms of managing conducted EMI/RFI. You are basically chopping the rectified AC input at a frequency that could be anywhere from a few tens of kHz to a few hundred kHz. In the interest of efficiency the rise and fall times are very short, so there is lots of high frequency content. Some PFC controllers operate at fixed frequency, others at variable frequency. I used to do designs using a controller that I ran at 100 kHz, which at the time was a reasonable compromise when FETs, rectifiers, inductor cores and inductor windings were considered (I often say that in switchers everything is in conflict with everything else).
Filtering ahead of the rectifier will certainly require a reasonbly "large" common mode inductor and some normal mode inductance might be necessary, too. I've seen designs using two common mode inductors.

Radiated EMI/RFI is always a concern in any switecher. Circuit layout needs to be carefully considered.

I noted that at some point in the video there was a huge amount of "fur" on the waveform shown on the oscilloscope.

text:
Interesting factoid about PFC: in the past, unscrupulous people used to tamper with their inductive loads, such as washing machines, pumps, and other motors and REMOVE the PFC capacitor in order to steal part of the electricity from the power company!
This is because power companies used to measure their customers' energy consumption using electromechanical meters, old devices containing a big spinning wheel that would complete a revolution after a known amount of energy was delivered to the customer, plus an odometer to count the wheel's revolutions.
One problem with those electromechanical meters (that has since been solved with digital energy meters) is that they would only measure the current delivered IN PHASE with the voltage. Large inductive loads, such as motors, were (and still are) required by law to be sold with a suitable capacitor as a passive PFC. But if one removed the capacitor, a good part of that load would become undetectable by the energy meter!
This is of course illegal and detrimental to the power grid, so nobody should attempt to do it, except in a laboratory condition.

text:
That device is called an on-line UPS. About $600+ for 3000VA. 
All alternators produce sine wave (also called "generators", although a generator technically produce DC). Square wave or "modified sine wave" is produced by cheaper inverters.
The problem with alternators are voltage spikes, under or over voltage, harmonic distortion (due to capacitive/inductive loads) and frequency deviation. This is caused by having a too simple regulating circuit on the alternator. 
You have 3 options.
1. As you stated, buy a generator set designed for electronic loads, with an AVR controller and/or an inverter.
2. Buy an on-line UPS. Usually at least as expensive as 1, but can be an alternative if you need a big gen. set with a lot of VA but only have a smaller electronic load. Gives a very good output. Best option.
3. Buy a line regulating UPS ("Interactive"). Cheaper and in my experience good enough in most cases. This is a bit hard to find for 2000W since you tend to get up to the PRO models with that power. If you can settle for a smaller 400-1000W you can find them in the price range $200-300. 
I have had a few UPSes blow due to voltage spikes, but the equipment survived due to the protection circuits in the UPS. This was in pretty extreme circumstances with a lot of nasty equipment running off the gen. set.

You can of course build something, which is a lot of fun, but very hard if you don't work with designing high power switched power inverters for a living. And it will likely not be cheaper.

text: Yes, PFC's perform well.  However, they have the same inrush problem on power application as putting a large cap directly across the input line.  In your demo board schematic the C2 cap is, effectively, across the input line if you trace back through the D1, D2, and bridge rectifier.  There is no real current limit when line voltage is applied.  Not even RT1 is wholly effective.  After the boost has time to charge C2 then everything works O.K.  This initial current will depend on where in the mains cycle the circuit is switched on.  I am finding that most of the LED lights with or without PFC have a large input cap that must be charged.  This external cap is effectively in parallel with C2.  The result can be a very large resulting cap that must be charged when power is switched.  An installation of several or many LED arrays can mean very high peak current.  I have measured hundreds of amps peak when an array is switched on.  Not every time, but always on the peak of the sine wave input.  This leads to very short switch life.  It also has the effect of "spot welding" and therefore oxidizing wiring splices or connections that do not have enough contact area.   I have stopped using the "clamp style" (Wago style?) splice devices because of this and gone back to twisting all connections and using a wire nut.  I wish the clamp type connectors were tested and rated for these conditions.  As for the switches?  Expect frequent failures.

It's shuffled between energy storage elements within the AC waveform cycle.   Inductive elements store energy in their core magnetic field, and capacitive elements store energy in the dielectric's electric field.  These elements cause current to either lead voltage or lag voltage.   The other type of element can correct power factor, since an inductor and capacitor combined at the right frequency, have zero net reactance, as the rest of the circuit experiences.

This causes the apparent product of current and voltage, to be more than the actual power that enters the electrical domain at the source, and exits the electrical domain to the load.

@eDoc2020  "Negative power factor" is a misleading term.  Even though cos(phi) is always positive for loads, and negative for sources, there is a sign convention that artificially adds another sign on top of the sign of cos(phi).

Quadrant 1 is inductive loads with positive reactive power (VARs), and quadrant 4 is capacitive loads with negative reactive power (VARs).   It's quadrants 2 and 3 that are sources, rather than loads.  Quadrant 2 supports capacitive loads, and quadrant 3 supports inductive loads.

IEEE assigns quadrants 1 and 3 as negative power factor, and quadrants 2 and 4 as positive power factor.
IEC assigns quadrants 1 and 3 as positive power factor, and quadrants 2 and 4 as negative power factor.

text:
Not by only a 555 - but a 555 is very convenient to use as the oscillator. Pin 4 connected to VCC, pin 2 and 6 is connected together, thru a capacitor to ground. Then a resistor (lets call it R1) is put between pin 3 (the square wave output) and the pin 2,6 (trigger and threshold). The frequency is set by capacitor and resistor values, 1 / (2 * C * R *0.693)
The capacitor then get a triangle wave over it, which can be connected to the non inverting input of a comparator - then the output of that comparator will be a PWM signal (that can turn on/off the MOSFET or IGBT via a gate drive), which is controlled by the voltage applied at the inverting input between 0% at 2/3 and 100% at 1/3 of the input voltage. 
To avoid the duty cycle reaching 100% (which will cause a boost converter to short out) an additional resistor (R2) can then be added between pin 2, 6 and 7 (discharge pin) on the 555 to bump up the duty cycle from 50% to a higher value that can set a maximum limit for the duty cycle by connecting the 555s output via a diode along with the comparator output to the gate drive - so each time the 555 goes low it pulls the gate drive low as well, turning off the transistor. Frequency is then set by 1 / (R1 * C * 0.693 + 1/(1/R1 + 1/R2) * C * 0.693) instead and the duty cycle will be R1 / (1 / (1/R1 + 1/R2) + R1). 

Then a signal that's composed of sine half waves (which looks just like what's coming from a rectifier without smoothing) in sync with the mains sine curve is applied to that non inverting comparator input. This will modulate the PWM from 0% up to maximum in the right way to perform nearly perfect PFC, if the inductor is big enough to run mostly in continuous conduction mode. 
I tried earlier to just take the signal from a separate rectifier and lower the voltage and adjust by resistors and capacitor and it worked quite well at high load (when the inductor stabilizes the current quite a bit), but got problem at lower loads with noise causing unwanted feedback that messes with the signal. I will try again later - maybe generate the sine half wave signal separately, then sync to mains by PLL. When I get it working I will put a video of it. It will be a quite high power one of 3+ kW - AC to DC power stage that I will use for other planned projects. 
I will not even start building things at those power levels without PFC - that's quite nasty on the grid and also means only like half of the available power on the fuses could be used.

Therefore a short spike of high current in every sinus wave doesn't mean high power. Think of PWM. The energy efficiency of the LED transformer is certainly quite perfect. A power factor correction means that you put I/U in phase, if it isn't - like for inductive loads. In your video we see (0:40) that I/U is in perfect phase, so this PFC circuit doesn't do anything in your case, except dampen the peak current a bit which has no effect at all to your power grid. You can have this cheaper and cleaner with a 50/60hz LC filter.

text:
The PFC circuit is pointless. A sinusoidal voltage and a sinusoidal current create a (1-(cos (2*Pi*f*t))²) power function which is of course not constant. How to achieve constant power (ie voltage) at the output, if the input power has a pulsating form?
This means that the PFC circuit cannot be a DC voltage pre-regulator as is often used. When it is a pre-regulator, it would have to draw constant power at constant consumption. And this would tend to create a current function of the form: I(t)=P/(A*sin(2*Pi*f*t)) which would draw a large current at low voltage points to maintain constant power. Such a current function increases the effective current through the conductors and creates additional transmission losses.
The best point of consumption for the smallest current through the conductors is at the top of the sinusoidal function. And the best PFC corrector is an LC filter after the diode rectifier, which suppresses the high harmonics of impulse current disturbances, i.e. reduces the current peak and extends the duration.

PFC only makes sense on machines that have sinusoidal current consumption that is out of phase with the voltage. And these circuits are called reactive power compensators.

There is also no conclusion from the measurement that the installation of the PFC circuit increased the effective input current by more than 10%. Because of this, losses in electricity transmission increase by more than 20%.

The glass analogy never works for me w.r.t. Power Factor... It explains a physical analog of real, apparent, and reactive power, how only real power is "useful" like the non-foamy part of the drink, but the existence of foam has no relevance to the existence of reactive power. 

If we could eliminate foaming from carbonated beverages without affecting their carbonation, we would. But the same isn't true for reactive power, which is absolutely necessary for induction to take place. Similarly, a correction to power factor does not eliminate reactive power, it just offsets for it with added capacitance.
